Subject: MSA + Order Form: proposed availability ladder and maintenance carveouts

Greg — attaching a redline of the MSA and the Order Form with our suggested TAU (target availability uptime) ladder and the service-credit matrix. Key points up front: 

- We propose a 99.95% target for Production (T0) and 99.5% for Non-Prod tiers; credits scale by 0.25% increments per your earlier ask. Details in the attached spreadsheet.
- Emergency maintenance: we can accommodate up to 6 hours/year for emergency security fixes with prior notice where possible; for true emergent patches that require immediate action we need a carveout without credits, but we will provide post-event RCA and credit consideration only if an ops error caused the outage.
- Response times: P1 — 1 hour ack + 2-hour remediation window; P2 — 4 hours ack, 24-hour remediation target. These are service-level response commitments (not SLA uptime triggers).

Can you confirm whether your procurement/legal team can accept the emergency-maintenance carveout language? If not, tell me which specific phrases block you and we’ll route to our legal for a call.

Attachments: ORBL_MSA_Redline_v2.docx (redline), OrderForm_TAU_and_Credit_Matrix.xlsx

Thanks — let me know availability for a quick 30-min alignment tomorrow.

—Marissa

Marissa — thanks for the redlines and the quick summary. A few clarifying points from our side after an initial read: 

1) 99.95% vs 99.9% — procurement will push for 99.9% on Production; can you run the cost delta/credit exposure for 99.9% so we can evaluate tradeoffs?
2) Emergency maintenance carveout: our legal is uncomfortable with a blanket no-credit position for emergency patches. They asked whether Redwood would consider a sliding credit where if emergent maint causes >30m downtime we trigger partial credit.
3) Response SLAs: ack vs remediation — we need clear definitions (what counts as acknowledgment, how uptime is measured during rolling mitigation).

Tara from Procurement is on cc, she’ll coordinate the formal redline passes. Could you loop in your legal? We’d like a live call next Wednesday afternoon PT to go through the MSA redlines line-by-line.

Marissa / team — suggested legal language below. This is intended to be compromise-first phrasing you can paste into the redline: 

"Emergency Maintenance. Notwithstanding any other provision, Provider may perform emergency maintenance to address security vulnerabilities or critical defects that materially threaten the security or stability of the Service. Provider will use commercially reasonable efforts to provide prior notice; when prior notice is not practicable, Provider will notify Customer as soon as reasonably possible. Emergency maintenance shall not automatically trigger Service Credits unless the Provider’s negligence or operational error is the proximate cause of the unavailability. If emergency maintenance results in an aggregate of more than thirty (30) minutes of measurable downtime in a single incident, Provider will (i) provide a post-incident report within five (5) business days, and (ii) grant Service Credits subject to the Credit Matrix in the Order Form, unless Provider reasonably demonstrates that the maintenance was required to remediate a security vulnerability or force majeure event."

A few notes: 
- This preserves the operational flexibility we need while giving the customer a path to credits if the event is protracted or our ops error caused it.
- We should define \"measurable downtime\" in the Order Form appendix (e.g., uninterrupted minutes of service unavailability as observed by our monitoring and customer-facing health endpoints).
- On 99.9%: Jonas, if we accept 99.9% for Production, we need to update the credit tiers (higher exposure) and discuss reserve capacity/autoscale policies. Provide cost delta/credit exposure and whether we can mitigate via stronger maintenance blackout guarantees.

If Greg’s team is agreeable to the above wording, we can propose it in the MSA redline and prepare a short one-pager for the Wednesday call.
